video_title: Crisis Is Coming In Early 2027 | Cem Karsan
gist: Recorded the day after a Democratic midterm sweep, Cem Karsan (auto-transcribed as 'Jim Carson/Croissant') and new Kai co-CIO Noel Smith argue that post-event vol compression and year-end structural flows make the tape supportive into January, but that a closed Strait of Hormuz, inelastic commodity inflation, a debt-refinancing wall and AI capex debt are pushing yields and credit spreads toward a breaking point. Karsan's big call is that the administration will allow a fast, crisis-like selloff starting around Q1 2027 (roughly January to March/April) so it can justify a historic rescue including equity buying via a sovereign wealth fund and Trump accounts; positioning is longer-dated puts/VIX/variance hedges plus debasement producers and 'strategic' US businesses.

themes.theme: Post-midterm vol crush and year-end flows

insights.claim: After the midterm election resolved, implied volatility collapsed, forcing dealers who were short stock against their options books to buy back hedges (e.g., going from 10 million to 6 million shares short), which mechanically lifted the market after an overnight drop.
insights.speaker: Noel Smith
insights.so_what: Event-driven rallies can be pure hedge-ratio mechanics rather than a fundamental 'all clear', so they should not be read as macro confirmation.
insights.quote: It's not that the market's giving an all clear because when is anybody ever said it's all clear, right? Nobody ever says that.

insights.claim: Skew was elevated into the election because investors bought downside puts and sold upside calls, leaving dealers short puts/long calls and short stock as a hedge; when the event passes and vol compresses, vanna and charm flows produce structural buying regardless of the election outcome.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: As long as an event resolves without contest, positioning implies a bullish drift afterward, independent of who wins.
insights.quote: Every single election for the last 20 years has seen positive flows coming out of it.

insights.claim: Post-election sector rotation showed defense stocks falling, rate-sensitive homebuilders rising, and some hyperscalers softening on fears they may not get the data centers they want.
insights.speaker: Noel Smith
insights.so_what: The Democratic sweep is being priced as negative for defense and AI data-center buildout and positive for rate-sensitive sectors.

insights.claim: Fed funds futures (ZQ) price only about 50 basis points of rate hikes between now and next September, down from more hikes earlier, which supports homebuilders and suggests the Russell 2000 has more upside than the Nasdaq-100 (QQQ) in a lower-rate environment.
insights.speaker: Noel Smith
insights.so_what: The market is in a hiking regime, not cutting; easing hike expectations favor small caps over mega-cap tech near term.
insights.quote: There's only 50 hikes or 50 bips of hikes priced into the marketplace between now and next September.

insights.claim: Rate volatility and equity volatility move together because lower rates improve creditworthiness and debt-servicing capacity, and equity is effectively a derivative of credit, so falling rate vol mechanically creates an equity bid.
insights.speaker: Noel Smith
insights.so_what: Watch rates vol (e.g., the bond market) as a leading input for equity vol and dealer flows.

insights.claim: Seasonal structural flows should support equities into year-end: positive flows into early/mid November, a window of weakness around Thanksgiving, strong positive December flows, then Christmas, as structured-product issuance keeps supplying vol and January LEAPS decay.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Fading the rally before year-end fights a structural tailwind for beta; the Thanksgiving window is the softer spot.

insights.claim: A January 1 re-leveraging effect, where gains and roughly 4.5% interest income must be redeployed into levered bets, is the biggest driver of the Santa Claus/January effect, and it is larger when markets are up on the year and growing as the options market expands.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Expect supportive early-January inflows, which also marks the point after which the risk window opens.

insights.claim: Karsan's three-legged framework for forward distributions is flows/positioning (dominant over days-weeks), macro (liquidity, rates, inflation, earnings growth), and policymakers' incentives (Fed, Treasury, administration), with the third leg far more important than usual under the current proactive administration.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Model short-horizon distributions with flows and multi-quarter distributions with macro and policy incentives; they can point in opposite directions simultaneously.

themes.theme: Skew and OPEX as crisis timing tools

insights.claim: Over the last seven years, equity skew has only been as high as now about twice, in roughly September-October 2019 and from around July 2021, and both episodes preceded rough markets (COVID crash 2020 and the 2022 decline).
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Current skew levels match prior pre-drawdown regimes, though Karsan cautions it is only three data points.
insights.quote: we've only seen skews this high broadly uh twice.

insights.claim: The COVID decline began the day after February 2020 monthly options expiration and ended the day after March quarterly OPEX, when dealer short-put open interest rolled off, showing that correct macro views only pay when positioning allows.
insights.speaker: Noel Smith / Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Options expiration dates are key timing windows for when a known macro risk can translate into a tail move.

insights.claim: Noel Smith knew about COVID in late December 2019 via Chinese colleagues and bought S&P puts and a Broadcom long-vol trade around Apple earnings, but the trade whiffed for about 60 days because the market ignored the risk while vol compressed.
insights.speaker: Noel Smith
insights.so_what: Being early with short-dated options on a correct thesis loses money; size up only when flows confirm.

insights.claim: During the March 2020 OPEX, Smith's clearing bank was begging him, a long-vol holder up a couple million dollars, to let them out of positions, illustrating dealer stress at the tail-event turning point.
insights.speaker: Noel Smith
insights.so_what: Peak dealer pain around expiration is a signal to monetize hedges.

insights.claim: Noel Smith says he has never made money trading off compelling narratives, citing shorting Herbalife on Bill Ackman's thesis only to watch it go straight up, and so he trades only positioning and math rather than political storylines like gridlock or impeachments.
insights.speaker: Noel Smith
insights.so_what: Political drama from the new Congress (impeachment talk etc.) is likely untradeable noise versus measurable positioning.
insights.quote: So, listening to cogent arguments and then trading off of them is not something I've ever been able to make money from.

insights.claim: Positioning is the one market input that can be measured accurately and has a direct one-to-one short-term price impact, whereas macro and policy views play out over quarters to years and correct longs often suffer poor price action before multiplying.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Combine a macro thesis with flow-based timing rather than betting big on the thesis immediately.

themes.theme: Hormuz, the petrodollar and inelastic inflation

insights.claim: Karsan has argued for nine months that the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen soon, because the conflict is about defending dollar-denominated commodity trade after China began trading with Iran and Venezuela in yuan, not about nuclear weapons.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Investors betting on a Hormuz reopening and an energy-price normalization may be wrong for a long time.
insights.quote: the simple fact is that we are in the Strait of Hormuz not because of nuclear weapons, but because of the US dollar.

insights.claim: Karsan views the US's worst-case acceptable outcome in Iran as a permanently closed Strait of Hormuz, which still preserves de facto US control of commodity trade in dollars, so the widely perceived US loss is actually consistent with its petrodollar objective.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Supports the view that the disruption is a policy-tolerated equilibrium rather than a temporary shock.

insights.claim: Karsan says the Houthis now allow only the United States free passage through the Bab el-Mandeb strait, so remaining Gulf-region trade is controlled by the US and settled in dollars, and he implies outside help enabled Houthi strikes on Saudi pipelines.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Under-discussed geopolitical arrangement that reinforces dollar dominance of commodity flows.
insights.quote: All trade currently is being controlled and managed by the United States of America, and it's being done in dollars.

insights.claim: With the Strait of Hormuz closed and inventories drawn to the bottom, commodity prices are approaching inelasticity, meaning supply-driven inflation across energy, diesel and fertilizer, with fertilizer cost effects likely felt in spring 2027.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Expect an inflation impulse into spring that pressures rates and food/energy-sensitive sectors.

themes.theme: Debt wall, AI capex and bond stress

insights.claim: Debt borrowed at near-zero rates in 2021 with average five-to-seven-year duration started hitting a refinancing wall this year across sovereign, corporate and municipal borrowers, creating a one-sided global supply-demand imbalance for debt.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Structural supply pressure on the long end of the curve independent of Fed policy.

insights.claim: Karsan says the administration anticipated the refinancing wave and passed regulatory changes he calls the 'strategic loan ratio' (likely the supplementary leverage ratio) and the stablecoin act to create more demand for Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Policy plumbing to absorb Treasury supply has already been used, limiting remaining easy levers.

insights.claim: The administration actively pressured hyperscalers into massive AI capex pledges, illustrated by Zuckerberg's hot-mic remark asking Trump whether $600 billion was the number he wanted, effectively giving these companies an implied government put.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: AI capex is partly policy-driven, so its continuation depends on government backstops rather than pure economics.
insights.quote: Boss, was that the the $600 billion the number you were looking for?

insights.claim: Oracle, led by administration ally Larry Ellison, has taken on debt at a scale Karsan calls irrational from afar, which he explains by an embedded administration put.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Oracle is a focal credit risk in the AI debt build, dependent on implicit government support.
insights.quote: Larry Ellison is one of the closest people in to the administration, has has basically mortgaged the whole business at scale.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler cash cushions went to zero this year and they shifted to massive debt issuance, which is pushing long-end yields higher, crowding out government debt, and starting to blow out credit default swaps and credit spreads.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: AI financing is now a direct source of rates and credit stress; watch hyperscaler CDS.

insights.claim: Karsan cites Elon (Musk) saying two weeks ago that all funding for neoclouds has dried up, signaling the AI financing pipeline is seizing.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Neocloud funding drought is an early crack in the AI capex chain; second-tier AI infrastructure is most exposed.
insights.quote: Elon has said, he said it 2 weeks ago, Neo Cloud's all funding for Neo Cloud's is dried up.

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.35%, at which point things started breaking, and the subsequent yield pullback was a de-risking flight to safety rather than a genuine improvement.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Roughly 5.35% on the 10-year is the demonstrated pain threshold for markets.
insights.quote: we got to 5.35 in the 10-year and stuff just started breaking.

insights.claim: The economy is in a catch-22: sustaining narrow AI-driven growth and current valuations requires ever more debt, which can only be sold at higher yields and wider CDS, building a cap on the market unless a larger entity backstops the debt.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Upside is capped without a policy backstop, making an eventual intervention the pivotal market event.

insights.claim: Karsan interprets Hank Paulson's surprise 45-minute Bloomberg appearance in April, warning of a coming debt crisis and calling for a facility to backstop the Treasury market, as a deliberate trial balloon for the coming policy response.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Signals that a Treasury backstop facility is being prepared, implying a run-it-hot, debasement outcome.

insights.claim: Karsan argues QE has never happened without a crisis, and backstopping corporate debt in today's populist environment (as the midterm showed) is politically impossible without one, so the administration will step back and allow a selloff, perhaps even give it a push, in order to rescue it.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Core thesis: a policy-tolerated crash is the precondition for the next massive liquidity injection.
insights.quote: I haven't seen We haven't seen QE without a crisis ever.

insights.claim: The administration has already run a create-a-crisis-then-resolve-it playbook twice, on Liberation Day tariffs and again in February-March around Iran, using vol expansion followed by sudden reversals to squeeze markets and drive liquidity.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Expect policy-driven vol spikes followed by abrupt reversals; buy the engineered panic once officials signal.
insights.quote: Create a crisis, resolve it, pump ball.

insights.claim: Karsan notes a hedge fund manager is Treasury Secretary and another heads the Federal Reserve, and argues they understand vol and flows as well as professional option traders and use them deliberately.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Policy timing will likely be chosen around flow windows, making flow analysis useful for anticipating policy moves.

insights.claim: Karsan predicts the crisis is most likely to begin in a January-March 2027 window, starting by around March-April at the latest, because Bessent prefers acting when flows make markets ripe, the last two episodes occurred in Q1, and losing control at year-end risks funding problems.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Hedges should be positioned to cover Q1 2027, with flows likely turning negative starting in January.
insights.quote: Q1 becomes a much more dangerous place from a flows perspective for the market.

insights.claim: To retain control, the administration will want the decline to be fast, within one or at most two quarters, because multi-quarter drawdowns force bank leverage-ratio deleveraging, and it wants the issue resolved by mid-to-late 2027 ahead of the 2028 election.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: The expected shape is a sharp, crisis-feeling crash (perhaps around 25%) rather than a slow 2022-style grind, favoring convex hedges.

insights.claim: Karsan expects the rescue to be larger than each prior one (2008, COVID) and to include unprecedented US government equity buying, though he expects the crisis itself to be less severe than 2008 because officials are managing price proactively.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Post-crisis environment would be strongly reflationary and debasing, favoring real assets and policy-favored equities.

insights.claim: Karsan flags that the Democratic midterm win has diminished the administration's control, and that China and corporate interests resisting government ownership stakes could make the managed decline get away from them, though the base case remains not to fight the Fed and Treasury.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Fatter left tail than the managed-crisis base case; size hedges for a scenario where rescue is late or insufficient.

insights.claim: Karsan says the positive year-end flows are not impenetrable: an administration attack on Iran or other risk-accelerating actions could trigger the selloff earlier than Q1.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Begin accumulating tail protection now rather than waiting for January.

themes.theme: State capitalism: sovereign fund and Trump accounts

insights.claim: The crisis would give the administration political air cover to create a large US sovereign wealth fund, possibly $5-10 trillion, with work underway on seeding it with Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac assets to leverage.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Fannie/Freddie and assets eligible for sovereign-fund purchase are potential beneficiaries.
insights.quote: I imagine Trump with a 10 trillion dollar or 5 trillion dollar sovereign wealth fund.

insights.claim: Trump accounts, which let the government buy stocks on citizens' behalf that cannot be sold for about 20 years, have expanded from children 12 and under to being required for 18 and under, with talk of extending them to age 40.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: A growing source of locked-in, price-insensitive equity demand.
insights.quote: The difference between left-wing populism and right-wing populism is right-wing populism you're they're going to buy stocks for you as opposed to send you money.

insights.claim: Karsan predicts US government equity investment will ultimately exceed $10 trillion over roughly a decade, a megatrend aimed at strategic businesses rather than broad S&P index buying, mirroring Japan's purchase of about 8% of the Nikkei.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Owning companies likely to receive state capital (with possible government stakes) is a decade-long theme.
insights.quote: We think this will be a, you know, ultimately $10 trillion plus of US equity investment.

insights.claim: The US government has already taken ownership stakes in companies such as Intel and MP Materials, and Treasury has bought back long-end debt and intervened in the yen, steps Karsan describes as boiling the frog toward larger interventions.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Precedent for direct state equity stakes; future rescue capital likely comes with government ownership terms that could dilute shareholders.

insights.claim: Karsan frames government equity buying as a way for the US to compete with China's non-profit-driven funding of solar, EVs, nuclear and rare earths, effectively adopting state capitalism with American characteristics.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Industrial-policy sectors competing with China are the probable targets of US state investment.
insights.quote: We're going to we're going to adopt uh socialism or communism with American characteristics.

themes.theme: Positioning: convex hedges plus debasement and strategic equities

insights.claim: Karsan recommends collecting long-dated puts funded by other positions rather than short-dated bets, avoiding the mistake of buying December protection and watching it decay, with flows likely turning favorable for the tail starting in January.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Concrete hedge structure: longer-dated, financed downside convexity covering Q1-Q2 2027.

insights.claim: Kai's hedging product combines S&P options, VIX options and variance futures (variance being volatility squared) to get extra convexity so that a volatility spike cannot fail to pay, addressing sequencing risk for investors.
insights.speaker: Noel Smith
insights.so_what: Variance futures provide nonlinear payoff in a crash, better than plain puts for tail protection.
insights.quote: the idea that volatility goes up and you don't make money is mathematically impossible.

insights.claim: For the debasement trade Karsan prefers equities of hard-asset producers such as gold miners, farmland, lumber and energy over the commodities themselves, because they pay embedded yield, are cheap after strong cash flows, and hedge better than outsiders.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Producers of real assets offer yield plus debasement convexity into a money-printing rescue.

insights.claim: Kai is rotating its equity book toward 'strategic' US businesses likely to receive government capital, which Karsan defines broadly as anything on the federal budget plus AI and AI infrastructure laggards and healthcare.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Look for under-performing names in government-favored sectors as rescue beneficiaries.

insights.claim: Karsan says the current window to be hedged is short, roughly seven to eight months, and if the crisis plays out Kai will aggressively monetize hedges and dramatically increase equity exposure at the bottom.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Plan both legs now: hedge into the crash, then redeploy cash and hedge profits into the policy rescue.
insights.quote: It's a very short window. We're really talking about seven eight months, right?

insights.claim: Karsan argues that the roughly 95% of investors long stocks and bonds hold a poor risk-adjusted portfolio at this moment, and that a liquid, diversified, convex portfolio is preferable until the opportunity presents itself.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Traditional 60/40 offers little protection in a rates-and-equity selloff driven by debt stress.

insights.claim: Noel Smith says a debasement and Bretton Woods-type unwind makes logical sense from both Austrian and Keynesian viewpoints and that his role is figuring out how to time and profit from it.
insights.speaker: Noel Smith
insights.so_what: Both partners share the structural debasement view; the disagreement is only about timing.
